title: Deleting Documents
subtitle: deleteOne, deleteMany, and safe deletion patterns
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Applications need to remove data — expired sessions, deleted user accounts, old log entries. But hard deletion is irreversible and can break audit trails, referential integrity, and analytics.
whyItExists.solution: MongoDB provides deleteOne() and deleteMany() for hard deletes, plus the common pattern of soft-delete (adding a deletedAt timestamp) for recoverable deletion. TTL indexes can auto-expire documents.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Hard delete for truly temporary data (sessions, caches). Soft delete for user data where you might need to restore, audit, or comply with data retention policies. TTL indexes for automatic expiry.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't hard delete if you need an audit trail, need to restore deleted items, or have referential integrity concerns (other documents referencing the deleted one). Don't use deleteMany({}) without double-checking — it's irreversible.

explainModes.beginner: deleteOne removes one matching document, deleteMany removes all matching ones. It's like selecting rows in a spreadsheet and pressing delete. But once gone, they're gone — which is why many apps use 'soft delete' (mark as deleted without actually removing).
explainModes.simple: MongoDB has deleteOne() and deleteMany() for removal. In production, most apps prefer soft delete — adding a deletedAt field — so records can be recovered or audited.
explainModes.standard: deleteOne() removes the first match. deleteMany() removes all matches. Both return { deletedCount }. For safety, prefer soft deletes in production. TTL indexes automatically expire documents after a set duration.
explainModes.technical: MongoDB delete operations acquire a document-level write lock. deleteMany() on large collections can be slow without indexes — MongoDB must scan. For high-volume deletes, consider bulk write operations or batching. Dropped collections are unrecoverable without a backup.
explainModes.deepDive: MongoDB does not physically zero-out deleted document space immediately — WiredTiger marks pages as reusable. Physical reclamation happens during compaction. The oplog records each delete as an idempotent 'd' operation. TTL index expiration runs a background thread every 60 seconds that calls deleteMany() with a filter on the TTL field.

content.text: MongoDB provides three deletion methods: deleteOne() removes the first document that matches the filter, deleteMany() removes all matching documents, and findOneAndDelete() atomically removes and returns the deleted document.
deleteMany({}) deletes ALL documents in the collection. The empty filter {} matches everything. Always double-check your filter before running deleteMany() in production.

In production applications, hard deletes are rarely the right choice. Instead, use a soft delete: add a deletedAt timestamp and filter it out in queries. This gives you an audit trail, allows recovery, and supports compliance requirements like GDPR data retention periods.

Create a partial index on deletedAt for efficient queries: db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { partialFilterExpression: { deletedAt: { $exists: false } } }). This index only covers active (non-deleted) users.
A TTL (Time To Live) index automatically deletes documents after a specified duration. Perfect for sessions, caches, temporary verification codes, and log retention.
MongoDB's TTL background thread runs every 60 seconds, so there is a slight delay between when a document expires and when it is actually deleted. Don't rely on TTL for precise second-level expiry.

a.name: Hard Delete
a.description: Permanently remove the document from the collection
a.useWhen: Temporary data (caches, anonymous sessions), data with no compliance requirements, or when you have full backups

b.name: Soft Delete
b.description: Mark as deleted with deletedAt timestamp, keep the document
weaknesses: All queries must filter deleted records
b.useWhen: User accounts, orders, transactions, any data that may need auditing or recovery

questions.question: What does deleteMany({}) do?
options: Deletes all documents in the collection
Throws an error — empty filter not allowed
questions.explanation: An empty filter {} matches every document, so deleteMany({}) removes all documents from the collection. The collection itself (and its indexes) remain.

questions.question: What is a soft delete?
options: Adding a deletedAt timestamp and filtering it out in queries
questions.explanation: Soft delete marks a document as deleted (usually with a deletedAt timestamp) instead of removing it. Queries exclude soft-deleted records by filtering { deletedAt: { $exists: false } }.

questions.question: What does a TTL index do?
options: Automatically deletes documents after a set duration
questions.explanation: A TTL (Time To Live) index automatically deletes documents after expireAfterSeconds seconds have elapsed since the indexed date field. Used for sessions, caches, and log retention.

faq.q: How do I drop an entire collection?
faq.a: Use collection.drop(). This removes all documents, all indexes, and the collection metadata. It is irreversible — there is no recycle bin. Always back up before dropping a production collection.

faq.q: Can I recover a deleted document?
faq.a: No — hard deletes in MongoDB are permanent unless you have a backup. This is why soft deletes (marking with deletedAt) are preferred in production. If you have an Atlas backup or a replica set oplog, you may be able to restore from there, but it's complex.

faq.q: How do I delete old data automatically?
faq.a: Use a TTL index: createIndex({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: N }). MongoDB automatically deletes documents where createdAt is older than N seconds. The background job runs every 60 seconds.

examples: TTL index on JWT token blacklist — auto-delete after token expiry time
Soft delete for user accounts with 30-day recovery window
Hard delete of raw ingest events after aggregation, keeping only the daily rollup
